scenes.narration: The genes do not care about Heart of Darkness; they care about copies. Heart of Darkness is an 1899 novella by Polish-British novelist Joseph Conrad, in which sailor Charles Marlow tells the story of his assignment as steamer captain for a Belgian company in the African interior. The novel is widely regarded as a critique of European colonialism in Africa, whilst also examining the themes of power dynamics and morality.

Take away the meaning and Heart of Darkness still functions — that is the disturbing part. Although Conrad does not name the river on which most of the narrative takes place, at the time of writing, the Congo Free State—the location of the large and economically important Congo River—was a private colony of Belgium's King Leopold II. Marlow is given an assignment to find Kurtz, an ivory trader working on a trading station far up the river, who has "gone native" and is the object of Marlow's expedition.

The unconscious does not argue with Heart of Darkness; it simply acts first. Central to Conrad's work is the idea that there is little difference between "civilised people" and "savages". The novella's setting provides the frame for Marlow's story of his fascination for the prolific ivory trader Kurtz.

Heart of Darkness feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. Conrad draws parallels between London ("the greatest town on earth") and Africa as places of darkness. Originally issued as a three-part serial story in Blackwood's Magazine to celebrate the 1000th edition of the magazine, Heart of Darkness has been widely republished and translated in many languages.

The bleak reading of Heart of Darkness is also the most testable one. In 1998, the Modern Library ranked Heart of Darkness 67th on their list of the 100 best novels in English of the 20th century. In 1890, at age 32, Conrad was appointed by a Belgian trading company to serve on one of its steamers.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about Heart of Darkness. While sailing up the Congo River from one station to another, the captain became ill and Conrad assumed command. He guided the ship up the tributary Lualaba River to the trading company's innermost station, Kindu, in Eastern Congo Free State; Marlow has similar experiences to the author.

The self that experiences Heart of Darkness is a committee, not a king. When Conrad began to write the novella, eight years after returning from Africa, he drew inspiration from his travel journals. He described Heart of Darkness as "a wild story" of a journalist who becomes manager of a station in the (African) interior and makes himself worshipped by a tribe of natives.

Reproduction explains more of Heart of Darkness than any philosophy dares to admit. The tale was first published as a three-part serial, in February, March, and April 1899, in Blackwood's Magazine (February 1899 was the magazine's 1000th issue: special edition). Heart of Darkness was later included in the book Youth, A Narrative; and Two Other Stories, published on 13 November 1902 by William Blackwood, although it was originally intended to be published in a Marlow trilogy, consisting of Youth, Heart of Darkness and Lord Jim.

Once you see Heart of Darkness as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. The Blackwood volume consisted of Youth: A Narrative, Heart of Darkness and The End of the Tether in that order. Researchers have suggested more than twenty prototypes for the character of Kurtz.

The story Heart of Darkness tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. Georges-Antoine Klein, an agent who became ill and died aboard Conrad's steamer, is proposed by literary critics as a basis for Kurtz. Conrad's biographer Norman Sherry judged that Arthur Hodister (1847–1892), a Belgian solitary, but successful trader, who spoke three Congolese languages and was venerated by Congolese to the point of deification, served as the main model, while later scholars have refuted this hypothesis.

Meaning is not found in Heart of Darkness — it is manufactured for it. Molly Mahood and others suggested that the Belgian soldier Léon Rom influenced the character. Peter Firchow mentions the possibility that Kurtz is a composite, modelled on various figures present in the Congo Free State at the time as well as on Conrad's imagining of what they might have had in common.

The cold light on Heart of Darkness leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. The "International Society for the Suppression of Savage Customs" is interpreted as a sarcastic reference to one of the participants at the Berlin Conference, the International Association of the Congo (also called "International Congo Society"). The predecessor to this organisation was the "International Association for the Exploration and Civilization of Central Africa".

Heart of Darkness did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. The novella opens on "the sea-reach of the Thames" where Charles Marlow tells his friends that "when the Romans first came here, nineteen hundred years ago" they would have sensed "the savagery, the utter savagery" surrounding them. Marlow then relates how he became captain of a river steamboat for an ivory trading company.

The honest version of Heart of Darkness starts by giving up the comforting part. He tells of his fascination as a child for "the blank spaces" on maps, particularly in Africa. The image of a river on the map particularly drew his attention.

Strip Heart of Darkness of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. In a flashback, Marlow makes his way to Africa by taking passage on a steamer. Marlow explores a narrow ravine, and is horrified to find himself in a place full of critically ill Africans who worked on the railroad and are now dying.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Heart of Darkness shows exactly where that breaks. Marlow must wait for ten days in the company's devastated Outer Station. Marlow meets the company's chief accountant, who tells him of a Mr.

What looks like free choice in Heart of Darkness is older than choice itself. Kurtz, who is in charge of a very important trading post, and is described as a respected first-class agent. Marlow departs with 60 men to travel to the Central Station, where the steamboat he will command is based.

Nobody designed the part of Heart of Darkness you experience — it was inherited. At the station, he learns that his steamboat has been wrecked in an accident. The general manager informs Marlow that he could not wait for him to arrive, and tells him of a rumour that Kurtz is ill.

Every serious account of Heart of Darkness eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. Marlow fishes his boat out of the river and spends months repairing it. Delayed by the lack of tools and replacement parts, Marlow is frustrated by the time it takes to perform the repairs.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of Heart of Darkness — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. The journey pauses for the night about eight miles (13 km) below the Inner Station. The steamboat is later attacked by a barrage of arrows, and the helmsman is killed.

The selfish-gene reading of Heart of Darkness makes it less romantic and far more precise. After landing at Kurtz's station, a man boards the steamboat: a Russian wanderer who strayed into Kurtz's camp. Marlow learns that the natives worship Kurtz and that he has been very ill.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. The Russian tells of how Kurtz opened his mind and how he admires Kurtz for his power and his willingness to use it. Marlow observes the station and sees a row of posts occupied by severed heads of natives.

The feeling that Heart of Darkness means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. Kurtz suddenly appears with his supporters who carry him as a ghost-like figure on a stretcher. The area fills with natives ready for battle, but Kurtz shouts something and they retreat.

Nothing in Heart of Darkness was built for you — it was built for reproduction. The manager tells Marlow that Kurtz has harmed the company's business in the region because his methods are "unsound". The Russian reveals that Kurtz believes the company wants to kill him, and Marlow confirms that hangings were discussed.

The psychology underneath Heart of Darkness is simpler and older than the story on top. Marlow threatens to harm Kurtz if he raises an alarm, but Kurtz only laments that he did not accomplish more. The next day they prepare for the journey back down the river.

Behind Heart of Darkness sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. The steamboat breaks down, and while stopped for repairs, Kurtz gives Marlow a packet of papers, including his commissioned report and a photograph, telling him to keep them from the manager. The next day Marlow pays little attention to Kurtz's pilgrims as they bury "something" in a muddy hole.

The nihilist does not deny Heart of Darkness — he only refuses to flatter it. Returning to Europe, Marlow is embittered and contemptuous of the "civilised" world. Several callers come to retrieve the papers Kurtz entrusted to him, but Marlow withholds them or offers papers he knows they have no interest in.

What culture calls destiny in Heart of Darkness is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. Marlow is left with some personal letters and a photograph of Kurtz's fiancée. When Marlow visits her, she is deep in mourning, although it has been more than a year since Kurtz's death.

When it was published as a single volume in 1902 with two novellas, "Youth" and "The End of the Tether", it received very little commentary from critics. Leavis referred to Heart of Darkness as a "minor work" and criticised its "adjectival insistence upon inexpressible and incomprehensible mystery".

Take away the meaning and Heart of Darkness still functions — that is the disturbing part. Conrad did not consider it to be particularly notable; but by the 1960s, it was a standard assignment in many college and high school English courses. Literary critic Harold Bloom wrote that Heart of Darkness had been analysed more than any other work of literature that is studied in universities and colleges, which he attributed to Conrad's "unique propensity for ambiguity".

The unconscious does not argue with Heart of Darkness; it simply acts first. Other critiques include Hugh Curtler's Achebe on Conrad: Racism and Greatness in Heart of Darkness (1997). The French philosopher Philippe Lacoue-Labarthe called Heart of Darkness "one of the greatest texts of Western literature" and used Conrad's tale for a reflection on "The Horror of the West".

In his 1975 public lecture "An Image of Africa: Racism in Conrad's Heart of Darkness", Achebe described Conrad's novella as "an offensive and deplorable book" that dehumanised Africans.

The bleak reading of Heart of Darkness is also the most testable one. Achebe argued that Conrad, "blinkered ... with xenophobia", incorrectly depicted Africa as the antithesis of Europe and civilisation, ignoring the artistic accomplishments of the Fang people who lived in the Congo River basin at the time of the book's publication. He argued that the book promoted and continues to promote a prejudiced image of Africa that "depersonalises a portion of the human race" and concluded that it should not be considered a great work of art.
